prompt: Which kind of tool runs the device's real operating system inside a virtual machine?
hint: The middle row of the table.

choices.text: Simulation, like Packet Tracer
choices.why: A simulation is a program imitating the device; the real operating system never runs.

choices.text: Emulation, like GNS3 or EVE-NG
choices.why: An emulator boots the vendor's own image, so the router answering is the real software.

choices.text: Kernel virtualisation, like Mininet
choices.why: Mininet's devices are pieces of one Linux kernel; no vendor system runs.

choices.text: A drawing tool for network diagrams
choices.why: A diagram runs nothing; it only shows the plan.

prompt: Match each tool to what is inside one of its devices.
hint: Imitation, real image, or the kernel.

pairs.right: A program imitating a Cisco device
A vendor image, run by a server you draw for
A vendor image, managed from a web browser
A namespace of one Linux kernel

right_distractors: A physical router in a rack

prompt: A colleague tried a new routing setting in Packet Tracer and it worked. What has that shown about the company's real routers?
hint: What was answering in Packet Tracer?

choices.text: That the setting is safe to apply on them
choices.why: The imitation is not their software; a default or a command may differ on the real version.

choices.text: That the idea works in Cisco's model of a router
choices.why: It proves the design in the imitation. The real routers' software still has to be checked, in an emulator with their image or on the devices.

choices.text: Nothing at all, since simulators teach nothing
choices.why: The concept was tested, which is worth something; it just is not proof about one device.

choices.text: That it works on every vendor's routers
choices.why: Packet Tracer models Cisco devices; other vendors were never in it.

prompt: What does Packet Tracer's simulation mode let you do that real equipment cannot?
hint: Time behaves differently there.

choices.text: Run real IOS images from any version
choices.why: Packet Tracer never runs IOS; its command line is an imitation.

choices.text: Pause time, one event at a time
choices.why: Each packet becomes an envelope you can pause on and open, layer by layer.

choices.text: Connect the simulated network to the internet
choices.why: That is GNS3's cloud node, which joins an emulated lab to a real interface.

choices.text: Measure the real speed of a cable
choices.why: Nothing virtual has a cable to measure.

prompt: A command a real Cisco router accepts is rejected by a router in Packet Tracer. What is the likeliest reason?
hint: What is behind that command line?

choices.text: The simulated router needs a licence key first
choices.why: Packet Tracer is free with an account; there is no per-device licence to unlock commands.

choices.text: Its imitation covers just what its courses teach
choices.why: Its command line is an imitation written for the courses, so commands outside them are missing.

choices.text: The command must be typed in simulation mode
choices.why: Simulation mode changes how time runs, not which commands exist.

choices.text: Packet Tracer runs an IOS version older than the router's
choices.why: It runs no IOS version at all; it imitates one.

prompt: Packet Tracer is downloaded, with an account, from Cisco Networking ___
hint: Where Cisco's courses live.

prompt: For which of these tasks is Packet Tracer the wrong tool?
hint: Whose devices does it model?

choices.text: Learning what a static route is
choices.why: A concept the courses teach, which Packet Tracer models well.

choices.text: Watching an ARP request flood a switch, step by step
choices.why: Simulation mode exists for exactly this.

choices.text: Testing a rule on the company's Juniper firewall
choices.why: Packet Tracer models Cisco devices only, and imitations at that; this needs the firewall's own software.

choices.text: Practising the IOS configure terminal commands
choices.why: The shape of the IOS command line is what its imitation is for.

prompt: Where do the router and firewall images for a GNS3 or EVE-NG lab legitimately come from?
hint: Neither tool ships them.

choices.text: From the vendor, under its licence
choices.why: The images are the vendor's software; GNS3 and EVE-NG only run what you are licensed to run.

choices.text: From the GNS3 VM, which includes them
choices.why: The GNS3 VM is the server that runs devices; it ships without vendor images.

choices.text: From any site that shares them, since a lab is not production
choices.why: Using software without a licence is not made legitimate by the use being practice.

choices.text: From Packet Tracer, which exports its routers
choices.why: Packet Tracer's routers are imitations; there is no real image in them to export.

prompt: How do you work with an EVE-NG lab?
hint: Several people can share one.

choices.text: Through a graphical client installed on every PC
choices.why: That is GNS3's arrangement; EVE-NG needs no client of its own.

choices.text: In a web browser
choices.why: The topology, the devices and their consoles all open in the browser.

choices.text: By SSH to each router, one at a time
choices.why: Consoles open in the browser; you are not limited to SSH.

choices.text: By dragging devices in Packet Tracer and exporting them
choices.why: The two tools share no file format for devices.

prompt: Ten routers of a current vendor image will not fit on a laptop in GNS3, while a ten-switch Mininet network starts in seconds on the same laptop. Why?
hint: What is each device made of?

choices.text: GNS3 draws its topology with heavier graphics than Mininet's command line
choices.why: The drawing is light; the devices are what consume the machine.

choices.text: Mininet's switches forward fewer packets per second than an emulated router
choices.why: Speed is not the issue; the GNS3 lab does not even fit.

choices.text: Each router is a VM with reserved memory; a node is a namespace
choices.why: Ten virtual machines each reserve memory for a whole operating system; ten namespaces share the one already running.

choices.text: Vendor images refuse to run on laptops
choices.why: They run wherever there is enough memory and processor; the laptop just lacks enough.

prompt: Which kinds of device can a GNS3 server run? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section lists three.

choices.text: Old Cisco router images, through Dynamips
choices.why: Dynamips emulates the hardware those images were built for.

choices.text: Anything that boots in QEMU, such as a router or firewall image
choices.why: QEMU runs full virtual machines, which is where modern images go.

choices.text: Docker containers, for light hosts
choices.why: Containers are the cheap way to add hosts to a lab.

choices.text: Packet Tracer's simulated routers
choices.why: Those exist only inside Packet Tracer; GNS3 cannot run them.

prompt: In the pingall run, how many pings did Mininet report as received?
hint: Read the Results line.

prompt: How many links would --topo linear,5 create?
hint: linear,3 made five: one per host, plus the line between switches.

prompt: With --topo linear,4 and --test pingall, how many pings would Mininet send in all?
hint: Every host pings every other host once.

prompt: At the mininet> prompt, what does h1 ping -c 2 h3 do?
hint: The first word is a host's name.

choices.text: Runs ping to h3 inside h1
choices.why: A command after a host's name runs inside that host; h3 is replaced by its address.

choices.text: Pings h1 and h3 from the machine running Mininet
choices.why: The command runs in h1, and only h3 is pinged.

choices.text: Asks the controller to send two packets
choices.why: There was no controller in this run, and hosts send their own pings.

choices.text: Joins h1 and h3 with two new links
choices.why: Links are made when the topology is built; ping only sends packets over them.

prompt: Which of these does a Mininet or namespace lab exercise for real? Choose all that apply.
hint: What is running inside a host?

choices.text: Linux's own handling of ARP and routing
choices.why: The hosts are pieces of a real Linux network stack.

choices.text: Packets you can capture with tcpdump
choices.why: tcpdump runs inside a host as it would on a server.

choices.text: A Cisco router's IOS command line
choices.why: Everything in the lab is Linux; IOS needs an emulator and a licensed image.

choices.text: A cable's signal and its faults
choices.why: A virtual Ethernet pair has no copper and no signal.

prompt: Mininet gave h1 the address 10.0.0.1 with a prefix length of /___
hint: Read h1 ip -br addr.

prompt: Match each part of the lab to the kernel feature lab.sh builds it from.
hint: Three pieces of the kernel, and one program.

prompt: sw1 lists its port as p1@if413. What is 413?
hint: The two ends of a cable name each other.

choices.text: The number of frames p1 has forwarded
choices.why: Counters are shown by ip -s link, not in the interface's name.

choices.text: A VLAN number assigned to p1
choices.why: No VLANs are configured in the office scenario.

choices.text: The interface number of p1's other end, in another namespace
choices.why: It is pc1's eth0, whose own @if412 points back at p1.

choices.text: The MAC address of p1 in decimal
choices.why: p1's MAC is printed in the next column, 02:b7:0a:5d:30:6c.

prompt: How many network namespaces did ip netns list show with the office scenario built?
hint: One per device.

prompt: Why does lab.sh up tear down whatever was there before it builds a scenario?
hint: Think of the transcripts in each lesson.

choices.text: Because namespaces cannot be renamed once created
choices.why: Teardown is not about names; a scenario could reuse them.

choices.text: So no lesson's output depends on an earlier lesson's leftovers
choices.why: Built from nothing, every scenario starts from the same state, and its transcripts can be reproduced.

choices.text: Because the kernel allows a single bridge per computer at a time
choices.why: Several scenarios have several switches, each a bridge.

choices.text: To free the memory held by the previous scenario's virtual machines
choices.why: There are no virtual machines; namespaces are cheap.

prompt: To run one command on one device of the lab: sudo bash lab.sh ___ pc1 ana 'ping -c 2 srv'
hint: The same word as ip netns uses.

prompt: Match each question to the place that can answer it.
hint: What has to be running for the answer to be true?

pairs.left: What does a switch do with a frame for an unknown MAC?
Does this rule work on our vendor's firewall?
pairs.right: An emulator with that vendor's licensed image

pairs.left: How long does OSPF take to reroute after a cut?
pairs.right: A kernel lab with FRR and a capture
The real cable, with a tester

prompt: Which of these questions needs real equipment, whatever lab you have?
hint: Which layer has nothing virtual to offer?

choices.text: Whether a switch port powers a desk phone
choices.why: Power over a cable is physical; no virtual port carries any (lesson 21).

choices.text: How a router picks between two routes
choices.why: Route selection is software, and any of the labs shows it.

choices.text: What a VLAN tag looks like in a frame
choices.why: A namespace lab can capture tagged frames, and lesson 19 does.

choices.text: Why a ping times out when the gateway is wrong
choices.why: Addressing and routing behave the same in a lab.

prompt: In lesson 3's ring, only 11 of 30 pings came back while OSPF found a new path. What does that number tell you about a real office network?
hint: Whose timers and whose hardware produced it?

choices.text: Its outage after a cable cut will also cost 19 pings
choices.why: Real timers, hardware and load differ; the lab's number belongs to the lab.

choices.text: OSPF loses about two thirds of all traffic
choices.why: The loss depends on the timers the lab set and the moment the cable was cut.

choices.text: Nothing at all, because labs are not real
choices.why: The mechanism is real: a cut, a gap while the protocol notices, then a new path.

choices.text: The shape of what happens, with that lab's timing
choices.why: The sequence is real kernel behaviour; the duration is a measurement of that lab.

prompt: Put the steps Mininet printed for the pingall run in order.
hint: Build, test, take down.
items: Add the hosts h1, h2 and h3
Add the switches s1, s2 and s3
Ping every host from every other host
Stop the links, the switches and the hosts
trap: The links come after both kinds of node: a cable needs something at each end before it can be laid.

prompt: A student with an 8 GB laptop wants to practise OSPF across six routers and capture the packets. Which fits best?
hint: Six of what, and in how much memory?

choices.text: Six vendor router images in EVE-NG
choices.why: Six full virtual machines of a current image are more than 8 GB can hold.

choices.text: Six routers on a whiteboard
choices.why: A drawing captures no packets.

choices.text: A namespace lab or Mininet, with FRR as the routers
choices.why: Six namespaces cost little memory, run a real OSPF implementation, and tcpdump captures the packets.

choices.text: Packet Tracer in simulation mode, with Wireshark attached
choices.why: Packet Tracer shows packets in its own window; there is no real interface to capture on.

prompt: A tool that boots a device's real operating system inside a virtual machine is called an ___
hint: GNS3 and EVE-NG are both one.

prompt: What makes every transcript in this course reproducible by a reader?
hint: Where did the lines come from?

choices.text: They were typed by hand from the lesson plan
choices.why: Typed output is exactly what the course refuses to print.

choices.text: They come from Packet Tracer's simulation mode
choices.why: Packet Tracer was not run; it imitates devices and prints its own model's output.

choices.text: A real kernel printed them, from a published script
choices.why: lab.sh rebuilds each scenario from nothing, and each captures.sh records what the kernel printed.

choices.text: Each one was checked on a Cisco router
choices.why: No vendor device was used; everything in the lab is Linux.
